Childcare research plays a vital role in improving developmental outcomes, educational readiness, health, and family well-being. This compiled collection of dissertation titles explores important areas of early learning environments, digital parenting, socio-emotional development, and inclusive childcare practices. Regardless of whether you are studying a psychology, education, or social work degree, these are topics that will enable you to develop and contribute to the well-being of children and their parents/carers.

Check out these outstanding childcare dissertation titles to spark your research journey!

1. Screen Time and Cognitive Development: Evaluating the Effects of Digital Exposure in Early Childhood

Focus: This research explores how varying amounts and types of screen exposure impact attention span, language development, and executive functioning in children aged 2–5, with a special focus on low-income households.

2. Attachment Styles in Nursery Settings: Investigating the Role of Key Workers in Emotional Security

Focus: Examines how consistent caregiver-child interactions in early childhood centres shape attachment behaviour, affect regulation, and social skills by the age of 4.

3. Inclusive Early Education: Barriers and Enablers to Integrating Children with Autism

Focus: Research identifies systemic, pedagogical, and attitudinal challenges to including children with autism spectrum disorders in mainstream nurseries, and proposes inclusive strategies based on case studies and teacher feedback.

4. The Effects of Parental Leave Benefits on Infant Care and Maternal Health

Focus: Investigates how parental leave, paid or unpaid, affects bonding, breastfeeding rates, and postnatal depression in mothers with cross-national comparative data.

5. Engaging Children in Outdoor Play and Physical Literacy: An Observational Study in Urban Context versus Suburban Context Preschools

Focus: Evaluate the differences with respect to gross motor development, attention span, and emotional regulation for children engaging in outdoor free play in both contexts.

6. Fostering Healthy Eating Habits in Early Childhood: Nutrition Education by Childcare Providers

Focus: This study will offer structured approaches towards nutrition education delivered by staff in nursery settings to explore its impact on early eating habits. In addition, the study will examine any changes in children’s food preference and Body Mass Index (BMI) and to gain knowledge about parental opinions related to children’s healthy eating choices.

7. Bilingual Language Development in Toddlers: A Longitudinal Study of Language Development and Identity Development

Focus: The purpose of the study ultimately will be to follow and trace the language development trajectory of bilingual children at age 2, 3, 4, and 5 years old. This study will examine vocabulary growth, code switching, language use at home, childhood identity development, and ways of demonstrating non-shifted or non-impulsive modes of speaking.

8. Stress and Burnout in Early Childhood Educators: A Study of Emotional Labour and Job Turnover

Focus: The study plans to examine several of the significant facets of burnout experienced by preschool/nursery educators. This research will investigate emotional considerations regarding the profession and workplace support contexts, and to what extent these may be tied to job satisfaction, stress, and turnover.

9. Male Engagement in Early Years Education: An Understanding of Fathers and Male Educators

Focus: This study will investigate the experiences and perspectives of men in early childhood care to explore how these men support the emotional development of children and whether they maintain and/or challenge gender norms influence primarily on roles and identities in caregiving contexts.

10. Ethical Dimensions of Digital Parenting: Surveillance, Trust, and Autonomy in Technology-Assisted Childcare

Focus: This research will evaluate the use of digital monitoring tools—such as parenting apps and wearable devices—on child autonomy, parent-child trust, and parental anxiety, especially among families using technology for remote supervision.
